They have now discussed a fish-shaped conference room in a temporary building, a story from the speaker’s childhood in Toronto, an interior and sculpture made for Jay’s offices, a performance piece created with Claes Oldenburg in Venice, chain-link fencing, a collaborative project that brought the speaker and another person’s ideas together through juxtaposed objects, metalwork developed with craftspeople, a back-and-forth design collaboration on a small dome and building, a Boston renovation that added a floor and carefully fit new details to the existing building, projects in Barcelona and Santa Monica, a laser laboratory at the University of Iowa featuring an abstract fish form, a small house in the West Valley, a house built along a stream that was dammed to make a lake, and a hospital for adolescents with schizophrenia at Yale. They have described a house next to Philip Johnson’s house in Minnesota, commissioned after Johnson was too busy to take on the owners’ project; designed as a sculpture to avoid resembling the estate’s subdivision. The speaker has discussed the house’s sculptural exterior and windows on the opposite side, and using Fin-Ply, a Finnish formed lumber, at Loyola’s chapel, where it did not work, while continuing to try to make it work. They now describe a site in Cleveland near Burnham Mall, noting that the mall was never completed, and point out new buildings by a lake, a railroad track, the city hall and courthouse, and the mall’s centerline as they discuss an opportunity to build on the site.

card.summary: The speaker is discussing architectural projects, emphasizing how buildings should fit their context and create comfortable, private, serene spaces. After showing projects in Santa Monica, Venice, and downtown Los Angeles, they described their 1960s paper-furniture work and its unexpected success at Bloomingdale's, then moved on to furniture experiments and failures. They have discussed the Japan building project and its construction, a fish-shaped conference room in a temporary building, a piece made for an exhibition at the Walker, a Toronto joke involving a bathtub and fish, and the Venice building developed with Jay Chiat and Claes Oldenburg; they then explained how frustration with available craft led them to use metal and junk-material art as models for a building that was itself a sculpture, before describing the Herman Miller factory complex in Sacramento, its central cafeteria space, and the speaker’s use of thin copper and galvanized panels to create an intentionally imperfect, stone-like appearance. They showed a billboard behind the cafeteria, called the composition “David and Goliath,” and described a Boston renovation that added a floor and drew on the neighborhood’s projecting cornices; they then discussed a Barcelona film-festival building inspired by the Hollywood sign, a small shopping center in Santa Monica, a windowless support laboratory at the University of Iowa featuring an abstract fish form, and a small house in West Valley whose form incorporates its mechanical equipment and pipe chase as a sculptural opportunity. They described building a house along a stream, damming it to create a lake, reflected on the poor workmanship and defensive approach prompted by building cheaply, and mentioned a hospital they were asked to design for adolescents with schizophrenia at Yale. They now describe a sculptural house for art collectors next to Philip Johnson’s house in Minnesota, with windows on the side away from the main house; it is made of metal and Fin-Ply, a formed lumber from Finland, which they had also tried unsuccessfully at Loyola’s chapel and are still trying to make work. They have moved on to a project in Cleveland, discussing Burnham Mall, its unfinished state, the surrounding lake and new buildings, and a site where they had the opportunity to build; they point out a railroad track, city hall, the courthouse, and the mall’s centerline extending outward.
